home-energy-audit.title: Home energy audits in Coquitlam: EnerGuide evaluations, costs and rebates
home-energy-audit.description: Book an EnerGuide home energy audit in Coquitlam: 30 licensed organizations, local prices, British Columbia rebates and what 55% pre-1991 housing means for your upgrade list.
home-energy-audit.lede: 30 NRCan-licensed service organizations deliver EnerGuide home evaluations in Coquitlam. Here's what one costs, what it tends to find in Coquitlam houses, and which British Columbia rebates it unlocks.

sections.h2: What an evaluation finds in Coquitlam homes
sections.html:
Of Coquitlam's 35,695 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 8% were built before 1961 and 55% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. The typical Coquitlam house dates from 1981–1990, and an evaluation is how you find out what that means for yours: the blower door measures air leakage, the advisor inspects the attic, walls, basement, windows and heating system, and the report ranks upgrades by what they'd save.

Coquitlam gets about 2,851 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −6.3°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Pitt Meadows. That's the 9th-lowest heating demand of the 70 cities we cover. The more heating a climate needs, the more each fix is worth, which is why the evaluation's ranked list matters more in some cities than others.

In the Vancouver area, 32% of households heat mainly with a forced-air furnace, 31% with electric baseboards, 12% with a boiler and radiators and 5% with a heat pump; natural gas is the main heating energy for 42% of households and electricity for 39% (Statistics Canada, 2023). The heating system on the report shapes the recommendations: a forced-air furnace invites a ducted heat pump, electric baseboards a ductless one.

There's no provincial price list; the City of Nanaimo quotes $400–$500 as typical for an existing home. Several B.C. municipalities subsidize evaluations for their residents (see local programs below).

Most providers quote the initial (pre-upgrade) and follow-up (post-upgrade) visits separately. Rebate programs that pay on measured improvement need both, so ask for the combined price.

• Initial evaluation, about 2–3 hours. The advisor measures and inspects the house and runs the blower door test.
  • Report and EnerGuide rating. You get the home's energy rating in gigajoules per year and a list of recommended upgrades with estimated savings.
  • Do the work. Most rebate programs only count upgrades done after the initial evaluation.
  • Follow-up evaluation. A second visit measures the improvement, which is what most rebates pay on.

sections.h2: Why air leakage matters in Coquitlam
sections.html:
Coquitlam gets about 2,851 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −6.3°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Pitt Meadows. That's the 9th-lowest heating demand of the 70 cities we cover.

Of Coquitlam's 35,695 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 8% were built before 1961 and 55% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older houses usually test leakier than newer ones, and an EnerGuide report compares your result with homes of the same era, so you can see whether your house is typical or a problem.

• Combustion safety. In the Vancouver area, the main heating energy is natural gas for 42% of households. A tighter house changes how fuel-burning appliances vent, so the spillage check should be repeated after serious air sealing. Combustion safety testing in Coquitlam
  • Radon. Sealing shifts the pressure balance between the house and the soil. In Health Canada's 2012 survey, none of the 109 homes tested in the Fraser North Health Service Delivery Area health region were above the guideline, a small sample that doesn't rule radon out. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 0.9% (1 in 113) of houses at or above the guideline for Vancouver Metro Area (Vancouver CMA). Test before and after big air-sealing jobs. Radon testing in Coquitlam

A blower door test is part of every EnerGuide evaluation rather than a separate purchase. There's no provincial price list; the City of Nanaimo quotes $400–$500 as typical for an existing home. Several B.C. municipalities subsidize evaluations for their residents (see local programs below).

• A calibrated fan is fitted into an exterior door and pulls air out until the house is at 50 pascals, the standard test pressure.
  • The result is air changes per hour at 50 Pa (ACH50): how many times an hour the whole volume of air would leak out and be replaced at that pressure.
  • While the fan runs, you and the advisor walk the house and feel for leaks at the attic hatch, rim joists, pot lights, trim and plumbing and wiring penetrations.
  • A second test after the work shows what changed, and it is what most rebates pay on.

The blower door test in detail.

heat-loss-calculation.title: Heat loss calculation in Coquitlam: sizing a heat pump for −6.3°C
heat-loss-calculation.description: A CSA F280 room-by-room heat loss calculation for Coquitlam homes, sized to the local −6.3°C design temperature: why it matters for heat pumps, what it costs and who does it.
heat-loss-calculation.lede: The heat loss calculation is how a heat pump or furnace gets sized for your house, and the key input is the design temperature: −6.3°C for Coquitlam, from NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Pitt Meadows.

sections.h2: Why the design temperature matters in Coquitlam
sections.html:
−6.3°C is the 10th-mildest design temperature of the 70 cities we cover. The F280 calculation works out how much heat each room loses on that design day, from the house's actual walls, windows, air leakage and ceiling insulation.

With a design day that mild, a heat pump sized to the calculation can carry most or all of a typical Coquitlam house's heating load, which makes sizing it right, rather than oversizing it, the main job.

In the Vancouver area, 32% of households heat mainly with a forced-air furnace, 31% with electric baseboards, 12% with a boiler and radiators and 5% with a heat pump; natural gas is the main heating energy for 42% of households and electricity for 39% (Statistics Canada, 2023).

Contractors who size by square footage routinely oversize. An oversized heat pump costs more to buy, cycles on and off, dehumidifies poorly in summer and wears faster. An undersized one leans on backup heat. The F280 report is the evidence either way, and it's worth having before you compare quotes.

About $150–$400 as a standalone calculation (a September 2026 planning range; quotes vary). Many energy advisors bundle it with an EnerGuide evaluation, which also gives the calculation measured air-leakage data instead of an assumption.

providers.heading: NRCan-licensed service organizations serving Coquitlam
providers.note: Many energy advisors also do room-by-room CSA F280 calculations for an extra fee; HVAC designers do them too. Ask for the F280 report itself, not just an equipment recommendation.

ventilation-assessment.description: Why Coquitlam homes get window condensation and musty air, what a ventilation and humidity assessment measures, and when an HRV or ERV makes sense. 26% of local houses were built since 2001.
ventilation-assessment.lede: Condensation on windows, musty basements and stuffy bedrooms are ventilation and humidity problems, and they're easy to confuse with insulation problems. A ventilation assessment measures which one you have.

sections.h2: Why Coquitlam homes get humidity problems
sections.html:
Coquitlam gets about 2,851 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −6.3°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Pitt Meadows. Mild, damp winters mean indoor humidity rarely has a chance to dry out on its own, so fans that actually vent outside matter.

Of Coquitlam's 35,695 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 8% were built before 1961 and 55% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Newer houses (26% of Coquitlam's were built since 2001) are tight and usually have an HRV or ERV that needs balancing and cleaning. Older houses that get air-sealed can lose the accidental ventilation they used to rely on.

• Relative humidity in living areas and the basement.
  • Actual airflow from bath and kitchen fans, and whether they vent outside rather than into the attic.
  • How much fresh air the house gets, and whether an HRV or ERV is balanced.

sections.html:
Of Coquitlam's 35,695 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 8% were built before 1961 and 55% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Attics in older houses commonly have a fraction of today's recommended insulation, and top-ups done over the years often buried air leaks instead of sealing them first.

Coquitlam gets about 2,851 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −6.3°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Pitt Meadows. radon-testing.title: Radon testing in Coquitlam: local levels, test kits and certified professionals
radon-testing.description: Radon in Coquitlam: Health Canada survey results for the Fraser North Health Service Delivery Area region, how to test for 3+ months, where to get kits and C-NRPP professionals locally.
radon-testing.lede: Radon is invisible, has no smell, and is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada. The only way to know about your house is to test it.

sections.html:
In Health Canada's 2012 survey, none of the 109 homes tested in the Fraser North Health Service Delivery Area health region were above the guideline, a small sample that doesn't rule radon out. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 0.9% (1 in 113) of houses at or above the guideline for Vancouver Metro Area (Vancouver CMA).

The two surveys aren't directly comparable: the 2024 study pooled about 69,000 volunteer tests and more of them were taken in basements, which partly explains its higher numbers. Neither can tell you about a single house, because neighbouring homes can differ widely.

• Use a long-term test of at least three months, with most of it in the heating season, which gives the most conservative result.
  • Place the detector in the lowest level you spend four or more hours a day in, away from drafts, and follow the kit's instructions.
  • If the result is above 200 Bq/m³, Health Canada recommends fixing it within a year, sooner if it's much higher.

Our full radon testing guide.

• BC Lung's library lending program puts radon detectors in many BC libraries, free with a library card, and the BC Centre for Disease Control publishes a BC Radon Map of results by area.
  • For a professional measurement or mitigation, search the C-NRPP directory by your Coquitlam postal code; it lists certified measurement and mitigation professionals.

sections.h2: Rules and help in British Columbia
sections.html:
• Since March 2024, the BC Building Code requires a radon rough-in in all new houses province-wide.
  • The Canadian Lung Association's Lungs Matter program offers up to $1,500 toward mitigation for households with low to moderate incomes or a lung cancer diagnosis.
  • If your level is high, mitigation (usually a sub-slab depressurization fan system installed by a C-NRPP-certified professional) typically costs $2,000–$4,000.

The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 0.9% (1 in 113) of houses at or above the guideline for Vancouver Metro Area (Vancouver CMA). Any home can have high radon, so Health Canada recommends testing every home.

faq.q: How long should a radon test take?
faq.a: At least three months, with most of it during the heating season. Short tests can't tell you your long-term average.

faq.q: Where can I get a radon test kit in Coquitlam?
faq.a: BC Lung's library lending program puts radon detectors in many BC libraries, free with a library card, and the BC Centre for Disease Control publishes a BC Radon Map of results by area. Hardware stores and lung associations also sell long-term kits for about $30–$60.

faq.q: What does radon mitigation cost?
faq.a: Typically $2,000–$4,000 for a sub-slab depressurization system installed by a C-NRPP-certified professional.

mold-testing.lede: Mold sampling tells you whether there's a hidden mold problem and roughly where. It doesn't tell you why, and fixing the moisture source is the actual cure.

sections.h2: Why mold shows up in Coquitlam homes
sections.html:
Coquitlam gets about 2,851 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −6.3°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Pitt Meadows. Mild, wet winters keep materials damp, so poorly vented bathrooms, basements and crawlspaces are the usual suspects.

Of Coquitlam's 35,695 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 8% were built before 1961 and 55% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older basements without a moisture barrier and houses that were air-sealed without adding ventilation are common trouble spots.

• You smell mustiness but can't find the source.
  • After a leak or flood, to check that cleanup worked.
  • Before buying an older house with signs of past water damage.

If you can see mould, you usually don't need a test to know it's there; you need to fix the moisture and clean it up properly.

No Canadian province has a mandatory mould standard for homes. Health Canada's guideline sets no numerical limit: it says to fix moisture problems and clean up visible mould.

Ask any Coquitlam tester which lab analyzes their samples, and look for one accredited under AIHA's EMLAP program for environmental microbiology. Pair sampling with a ventilation and humidity assessment, which finds the cause.

Ventilation and humidity assessments in Coquitlam · Our mold and indoor air quality guide

faq.q: How much does mold testing cost in Coquitlam?
faq.a: Plan on about $300–$600 for a typical sampling visit (a September 2026 planning range); lab fees for extra samples add to that.

faq.q: Do I need a test if I can see mould?
faq.a: Usually not. Visible mould needs cleanup and a fix for the moisture source. Testing helps most when you suspect mould you can't see.

faq.q: Is there a legal mould limit for homes in Canada?
faq.a: No. Health Canada sets no numerical limit; its guidance is to control moisture and clean up mould. Quebec has a voluntary handling standard.

sections.html:
Of Coquitlam's 35,695 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 8% were built before 1961 and 55% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Vermiculite attic insulation: loose, pebbly, grey-brown or silver-gold granules.

B.C. has Canada's strictest regime: before renovation or demolition work, a qualified person must inspect and sample for hazardous materials such as asbestos and lead (OHS Regulation s. 20.112), and since January 1, 2024, asbestos abatement contractors must be licensed by WorkSafeBC.

Whatever the rules, don't sand, cut or remove suspect material yourself before it's tested.

A trained assessor takes small samples, and an accredited lab analyzes them; plan on about $50–$150 per sample. Asbestos labs in Canada are typically accredited under NIST's NVLAP program.

sections.h2: Which Coquitlam homes are at risk
sections.html:
Of Coquitlam's 35,695 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 8% were built before 1961 and 55% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Built before 1960: probably has lead-based paint (Health Canada).
  • Built 1960–1990: exterior paint may contain lead, and interior paint may contain smaller amounts.
  • Built after 1990: consumer paints were virtually lead-free by then.

• Swab kits ($15–$40) give a quick screen of the surfaces you plan to disturb.
  • For certainty, send paint chips to a lab accredited under AIHA's ELLAP program, or hire a firm with an X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyzer.
  • Test before sanding, stripping or replacing old windows and trim.

Our lead paint guide.

Don't dry-sand, use a heat gun or power-wash it. Contain the work area, mist surfaces, clean with a HEPA vacuum, and keep children and pregnant people away until cleanup is done. No province has a lead-paint rule aimed at homeowners, but contractors in B.C. and Yukon must include lead in pre-renovation or demolition hazard inspections.

faq.a: They are a useful screen. For renovation decisions, confirm with a lab analysis of paint chips or an XRF reading.

commercial-energy-audit.description: Commercial and multi-unit building energy audits in Coquitlam: ASHRAE levels, no mandatory reporting rule, and 7 utility or government incentives for audits and studies.
commercial-energy-audit.lede: Offices, apartment buildings, retail and industrial sites get engineering energy audits rather than EnerGuide evaluations. Here's what applies in Coquitlam: no mandatory reporting rule and 7 incentive programs we found for audits and studies.

sections.h2: Reporting rules that apply in Coquitlam
sections.html: • No city-specific rule found (none found): No municipal energy/water benchmarking, reporting or building-performance by-law found; provincial rules apply (see rules.provinces.BC).

• Integrated energy audit (BC Hydro): Up to 100% funding for an energy expert (Alliance of Energy Professionals member) to audit a whole facility or selected systems; payment usually goes directly to the energy expert. Details
  • Feasibility study (BC Hydro): Study 100% funded when the opportunity exceeds 200,000 kWh/yr or 100 kW; 50% funded for 25,000-200,000 kWh/yr or 25-100 kW (efficiency, efficient electrification or demand response). Details
  • Continuous Optimization (C-Op) program (BC Hydro in partnership with FortisBC): Funding of up to $0.15 per sq ft for an approved service provider to retro-commission or recommission HVAC and other systems; 75% is paid after the investigation stage and 25% on completion. Details
  • Commercial Energy Assessment Program (FortisBC): Free walkthrough energy assessment by a FortisBC-authorized consultant, with a report within 60 days listing low/no-cost measures, possible upgrades and applicable FortisBC rebates. Details
  • Custom Efficiency Program - energy study funding (FortisBC): Up to 50% of an energy study by a FortisBC-approved consultant (max $20,000 for commercial buildings), plus an implementation bonus of up to another 50% of the study cost (max $20,000) once approved measures are installed. Implementation incentives: the lesser of $6/GJ (gas) or $0.03/kWh (electric) over measure life, 75% of invoiced costs, or $500,000 for commercial buildings. Details
  • Energy efficiency for rental apartments and accommodations program (FortisBC): Free building energy assessment by FortisBC engineering consultants plus free in-suite showerheads, aerators, pipe insulation and hot-water recirculation controls, with ongoing support for larger upgrades. Details
  • Energy-saving support for small businesses program (FortisBC with GreenStep Solutions): Free customized energy advice (15-30 minute consultation by phone, video or in person), which may include a basic energy assessment and rebate information, with a follow-up email. Details

• Level 1, walk-through: a site visit and bill review that benchmarks the building and lists low-cost measures.
  • Level 2, energy survey and analysis: where the energy goes, with savings and cost estimates per measure. Most incentive applications use this level.
  • Level 3, detailed analysis: monitoring and modelling for capital-intensive projects.

Ask which level a quote covers. Audits are done by engineering firms and energy consultants; look for a P.Eng. and credentials such as the Certified Energy Manager (CEM). How commercial energy audits work.
